title: Leadership training in healthcare: a systematic umbrella review
actual_read_scope: Methods; Results evaluation/quality/impact; Discussion limitations; not all supplements or underlying reviews
short_exact_passage: few studies employed observer assessments, control groups or included long-term follow-up

appraisal.population: Healthcare students and professionals, including undergraduates; broader than adult employees.
appraisal.search: Methods report database searches on 20 June 2024; abstract says reviews before October 2024. Preserve this date discrepancy.
appraisal.included: 86 reviews; 52 systematic. At least 1,659 unique underlying articles; exact total unavailable.
appraisal.quality: 35 low, 9 unclear and 42 high risk under ROBIS. Single data extractor; human plus ChatGPT appraisal. ROBIS was not adapted for nonsystematic reviews.
appraisal.findings: 36/86 reviews reported behaviour and 30/86 organisational or clinical outcomes. These count reporting coverage, not effectiveness.
appraisal.contrary: Neutral and negative findings rarely examined. Absence of negative overall conclusions does not demonstrate no harm.
appraisal.causal_limit: Narrative umbrella synthesis; programme-component associations are not causal component effects.
appraisal.overlap: Lyons 2021 and Mianda & Voce 2018 are cited in its bibliography. Exact primary-study overlap not crosswalked. No independent replication count.

title: Developing and evaluating clinical leadership interventions for frontline healthcare providers: a review of the literature
actual_read_scope: Methods; results evaluation section/Table6; limitations and discussion; not every intervention-table cell
short_exact_passage: Only one study included an evaluation at all four levels

appraisal.population: 24 papers on frontline healthcare providers, English 2004–2017; all studies in high-income settings.
appraisal.search: Google Scholar, EBSCOhost, named databases and references; includes peer-reviewed and grey literature.
appraisal.quality: StaRI reporting checklist; descriptions generally poor. Reporting completeness does not establish low causal bias.
appraisal.findings: Nine studies used pre/post assessments; most used post-only evaluations. One assessed all four Kirkpatrick levels.
appraisal.causal_limit: Pre/post and 360-degree assessment improve information but do not establish attribution without adequate comparisons.
appraisal.overlap: Cited in the 2025 umbrella; exact primary overlap with Lyons not assessed.

title: Evidence-based medical leadership development: a systematic review
actual_read_scope: Main article Methods pp206–208; Results reliability and taxonomy pp208–210; Discussion limitations p211; supplements not fully appraised
source_section_page_or_line: PDF pages2–3 Methods/Results; page3 lines57–75,108–152; page5 lines50–61; page6 lines32–116
short_exact_passage: 92% did not include a control group

appraisal.population: 117 studies, English peer-reviewed 2000–January 2020, physicians at least 10% of learners.
appraisal.search: MEDLINE, extensive reference/citation search, and re-examination of the Frich review dataset.
appraisal.quality: 28 studies classified higher reliability under authors’ MERSQI/JBI thresholds. These are appraisal cutoffs, not training success criteria.
appraisal.findings: 46% post-only; 60% solely self-report; 9 controlled studies, only 1 randomised. Taxonomy separates self-reported/observed behaviour and results.
appraisal.causal_limit: Mentoring, project-work and faculty associations across programmes are not randomised component comparisons. Heterogeneity precluded pooling; positive publication bias possible.
appraisal.overlap: Explicitly updates Frich’s dataset and is cited in the 2025 umbrella. Do not count these as independent primary replications.

title: Leadership training design, delivery, and implementation: A meta-analysis
actual_read_scope: Methods pp1693–1695; Tables1–2; Results overview; limitations pp1703–1704; targeted bibliography snowball; not full moderator tables/supplementary primary coding file
source_section_page_or_line: PDF page8 lines74–107,page9 lines19–42,89–117,page10 lines13–63,page19 lines1–30
short_exact_passage: our results may still be upwardly biased

appraisal.population: 335 independent adult-employee samples, N=26,573; students excluded; earliest usable study 1951; searches through December 2014.
appraisal.search: PsycINFO, Business Source Premiere, ProQuest dissertations, Google Scholar and prior-review references; published and unpublished studies.
appraisal.outcomes: Reactions; learning; on-job transfer from self/supervisor/peer/subordinate ratings; organisational or subordinate results. Outcome level does not specify causal strength.
appraisal.designs: Table 1: 208 repeated-measures, 62 independent-groups and 58 independent-groups with repeated-measures. Counts do not sum to 335; do not repair silently or assume randomisation.
appraisal.reported_estimates: Authors’ corrected delta: learning .73 (95% CI .62–.85); transfer .82 (.58–1.06); results .72 (.60–.84); reactions .63 (.12–1.15). No new pooling or numerical recomputation.
appraisal.causal_limit: Mixed designs, statistical design conversions and an imputed average pre/post correlation. Moderators are associations. Broad averages do not guarantee a particular programme works.
appraisal.bias: Publication-bias tests found no evidence, but authors explicitly acknowledge unavailable ineffective programmes could bias results upward.
appraisal.overlap: Kawakami 2006 is an explicitly starred included reference on PDF page 27. The primary trial and meta-analysis are not independent confirmations.

title: Evaluation of iLead, a generic implementation leadership intervention: mixed-method preintervention–postintervention design
short_exact_passage: the boosting effect of the contextualisation, which should facilitate a transfer of training for group 2, was absent

appraisal.population: 52 Swedish regional healthcare managers: 21 individualised, 31 contextualised.
appraisal.intervention: Five half-day workshops on four occasions; full-range leadership model; practice, role-play and action plans. Contextualised group shared an implementation case plus senior-manager training.
appraisal.comparison: Nonrandom organisational assignment to two training versions; no untreated control. Contextualised group attendance mandatory, with a common case.
appraisal.timing: Figure 1: baseline November/December 2015–January 2016; workshops January–June 2016; follow-up 1 June 2016; follow-up 2 November/December 2016–January 2017.
appraisal.attrition: Manager attrition 11 versus 4; falling employee response rates and unit turnover; only a small group followed at all three times.
appraisal.analysis: Multilevel models address repeated observations and employee/group nesting; they do not eliminate allocation confounding.
appraisal.findings: High satisfaction and improved perceived knowledge; retrospective employee reports of improvement; no contextualisation advantage on implementation leadership.
appraisal.causal_limit: No randomisation or untreated control; active implementation behaviour measured only at the two follow-ups, with no baseline. Knowledge self-rated; retrospective change vulnerable to bias.
appraisal.organizational_outcomes: No objective implementation, patient outcome or ROI demonstration.
appraisal.adverse: Interviews describe frustration with the mandated implementation case and concurrent reorganisation. These contextual explanations are not proven treatment-effect moderators.

title: Online training to improve evidence-based leadership competencies among nurse leaders in China: a feasibility randomised controlled trial
short_exact_passage: No statistically significant differences were found in other scores

appraisal.population: 119 nurse leaders in two Chinese tertiary hospitals: 59 intervention, 60 active control.
appraisal.intervention: Seven modules, planned seven months; actual nine months following COVID interruption. Recorded lectures, tasks on own leadership problem, tutors and peers.
appraisal.comparison: Individual 1:1 computer block randomisation, block size 6, remote allocation. Same topics/modules/duration in control; independent study without assistance and with different tasks.
appraisal.blinding: Participants/researchers unblinded; statistician blinded. Contamination possible.
appraisal.timing: Pre-training baseline in 2022; post-test 16–30 May 2023. No distant post-training follow-up.
appraisal.attrition: 22 dropouts: 9/59 versus 13/60. Table 4 uses n=50/47. Claimed ITT/no missing appears to mean no missing within returned instruments; exact ITT handling unclear.
appraisal.outcomes: Primary feasibility: logins, tasks, dropout. Secondary potential effectiveness: self-rated MLQ, EBPQ, self-efficacy, self-esteem, intention to leave and feedback.
appraisal.findings: Course feedback positive in both arms. Most between-arm efficacy outcomes null. Avoidant leadership subscale lower (p=.039 rank test/.048 mean test); multiple outcomes with no adjustment stated.
appraisal.causal_limit: Feasibility study without efficacy sample-size calculation; mostly self-ratings; isolated secondary finding needs replication. No independent behaviour, follower or patient outcomes.
appraisal.harm: No adverse-event monitoring reported. Frustration/dropout explanations in discussion are not measured harm effects.

title: The Effects of a Principal Professional Development Program Focused on Instructional Leadership
short_exact_passage: decreased the amount of instructional support and feedback teachers reported receiving

appraisal.population: 100 elementary schools, 8 districts, 5 states; 100 principals, 3,266 teachers, 23,923 students. Project website says 10 districts; use report’s 8.
appraisal.intervention: CEL instructional leadership; intended and delivered 188 hours over two years, including 100 hours coaching; 2015–16 and 2016–17.
appraisal.comparison: School randomisation within district matched pairs, 50 per arm. Control had usual district professional development. Volunteer districts had no existing intensive principal programme.
appraisal.timing: Outcomes during both training years; retention and student achievement again in year 3 (2017–18), one year after programme. Three districts lacked year-3 data.
appraisal.outcomes: Principal and teacher surveys, principal time logs, administrative tests and retention. Actual quality of feedback/instruction not directly observed.
appraisal.findings: No average achievement improvement; most climate and retention outcomes null. Teachers reported support/feedback about two fewer times annually. Some negative perceptions and first-year retention effect.
appraisal.causal_limit: Randomised offer strengthens attribution for this programme and population. Generalisation limited; year-3 missing districts; multiple outcomes. Technical appendices not read, so cluster standard errors/precision not appraised here.
appraisal.implementation: All 188 hours delivered on average; 84% original principals stayed two years. Replacements offered training; one school did not participate in year 2.
appraisal.status: Authoritative government report, not a peer-reviewed journal article; eligibility clarified by lead protocol v4.

title: Effects of Web-Based Supervisor Training on Job Stressors and Psychological Distress among Workers: A Workplace-Based Randomized Controlled Trial
actual_read_scope: Methods and results, PDF pp29–31;Discussion limitations p33;Tables 1–2 in text extraction;no independent numerical recomputation
short_exact_passage: may be trivial and attributable to multiple testing

appraisal.population: Eight Japanese sales/service workplaces, four per arm; 23 supervisors per arm; 81/108 subordinate complete cases.
appraisal.intervention: Web mental-health supervisor training, nine chapters, about 3–5 hours over four weeks; 22/23 completed.
appraisal.comparison: Workplace randomisation by random-number table. Control supervisors received two hours of relaxation training; abstract “non-training” label is incomplete.
appraisal.timing: November 2002 baseline; immediate post-test manager knowledge; February 2003 subordinate follow-up, three months after training.
appraisal.outcome_specific_design: Manager knowledge/attitudes assessed only in training arm, n=16 paired analysis. Subordinate BJSQ measured at baseline and follow-up in both arms.
appraisal.analysis: Authors call analysis ITT, but exclude 7 workers after one supervisor’s death and nonresponders. Repeated ANOVA at worker level; no explicit cluster correction in described Methods.
appraisal.findings: Some uncontrolled perceived-knowledge gains. No effects on BJSQ stressor, support or distress scales. Two positive individual-item effects; authors flag possible multiplicity artefacts.
appraisal.reliability: BJSQ alpha .54 interpersonal conflict; .65–.75 other stressor scales; .81–.84 support; .92 distress.
appraisal.causal_limit: Only eight clusters and baseline imbalance; subjective outcomes and possible expectations. Controlled-trial label must not be applied to the uncontrolled learning outcome.
appraisal.harm: One supervisor died during follow-up; no attribution to training reported. Do not label as a training adverse event.
appraisal.overlap: Explicit included reference in Lacerenza 2017; separate named 2005 trial is not assumed the same sample.

lead_review_caution: Methods reports16 supervisors for learning comparison, Table1 caption19; exact learning denominator unresolved. Do not inherit controlled worker-outcome comparison for training-arm-only learning ratings.

title: Developing engaged and ‘teamful’ leaders: A randomized controlled trial of the 5R identity leadership program
discovery_route: S4 identity/shared leadership refinement; search result S4 -> PLOS printable
review_overlap_note: ILI foundation cited/adapted. Earlier5R/5RS evaluations cited in introduction are separate samples, not independent confirmations extracted here.
participants_and_setting: 76 leaders of teams with >=2 members; about70% construction/manufacturing; 43 gaveT2 data. Twelve cohorts; senior/intermediate leaders.
training_goal: Knowledge/skills of social identity leadership and healthy inclusive team functioning; individual leader-identity pursuit deliberately distinct.
theory_or_change_model_explicit: Social identity approach; building shared we/us identity.
content_and_delivery: Five online modules around1h each, two weeks apart; videos, case, reflection and activities with own teams. Facilitated arm additional90min workshops each; self-directed arm same modules without workshops.
dose_and_duration: Approximately two months; facilitators had20h preparation.
assignment_and_comparator: Stratified block randomization of12 cohorts among facilitated(n27), self-directed(n22), waitlist(n27). Published analyses use individual repeated-measures ANOVA; no cohort adjustment stated.
baseline_and_followup: T1 before; T2 at programme end (~2months); no later durability measure.
attrition_and_missingness: 43/76 completedT2:18/27 facilitated,9/22 self-directed,16/27 control. Completer main analyses; ITT using mean or last-observation-carried-forward imputations reported.
blinding_or_independent_rating: Participant leader self-report; no follower outcomes collected. Waitlist comparator does not equalize expectancy/attention.
implementation_fidelity: Activities with teams required; no independent observation of activity delivery documented.
validity_bias_negative_findings: Self-rated knowledge is agreement with knowing how to lead, not a scored test. Data-derived team composites in small sample; reliability is not causal or construct validation. Null organizational alignment and no detected advantage of facilitated mode on target outcomes. Reduced personal leader-identity pursuit in facilitated arm reflects programme aim rather than automatic harm/success. Authors disclose commercial/IP interests. Authors' claim that control-variable pattern rules out common-method bias is stronger than these data warrant.

source_passages.excerpt: evidence of 5R’s efficacy would not be based exclusively on the self-reports of participants.

outcomes.operational_definition: Agreement that one knows how to produce team cohesion/identity;1–7agreement. Table1 example concerns knowing how to create team cohesion.
outcomes.reliability: No alpha for this3-item scale located; composite alphas below are separate.
outcomes.validity: ILI citation supports construct ancestry; adaptation to self-knowledge requires fresh validity/behaviour corroboration.
outcomes.result: Treatment mean5.59->6.19 vscontrol5.80->5.65; reported Time×ConditionF(2,41)=10.19,p<.001,partialeta2=.20. These printed degrees of freedom may warrant review; effect not a knowledge-exam score.

outcomes.measure: Average of team reflexivity(4items), psychological safety(3), goal clarity(3), inclusive climate(4)
outcomes.operational_definition: Leader perception of deliberation, speaking-up, clear shared goals and sought input. Components generally1–7agreement/accuracy.
outcomes.validity: Data reduction using10team measures in small sample; authors did not use PCAfactor scores.
outcomes.result: Treatment5.80->6.16,control5.91->5.92; reported interactionp=.045. Not independent team-member evidence.

outcomes.construct: Team engagement; organizational alignment; leader identity pursuit
outcomes.measure: Engagement composite(team identification1item,OCB4,work engagement9,team efficacy5); alignment(organizational identification1,goal clarity3); pursuit4items
outcomes.operational_definition: Personal group identification/helpfulness/job engagement/collective efficacy and organizational alignment; pursuit captures establishing oneself as the leader.
outcomes.result: Engagement rose in treatment(reported interactionp=.016); alignment no detected effects(allF<1). Pursuit treatment4.67->3.62 vscontrol4.88->4.69, especially facilitated. Bootstrap indirect path to teamfulness reported but not engagement.

lead_review_caution: Source narrative/table statistical inconsistencies, cohort assignment versus individual analysis and imputation issues remain unresolved. Preserve specialist-reported values as source extraction, not verified quantitative conclusions. Report uses author-direction summary with these limitations.

title: Combining a leadership course and multi-source feedback has no effect on leadership skills of leaders in postgraduate medical education. An intervention study with a control group
review_overlap_note: Cites priorMSF developmental-plan study DOI10.1111/j.1365-2923.2008.03259.x; prior validation not independently appraised.
participants_and_setting: Consultants responsible for postgraduate medical education(CRE), Danish hospitals. Course evaluation40/42; baselineMSF27 intervention/15control; followup20/9.
content_and_delivery: Seven-day course:two3-day residential modules plus followupday, over6months; curriculum includes educational culture,planning,supervision,implementation,communication,personal development. Two mandatory departmental plans.
assignment_and_comparator: Nonrandom convenience course participants vsdepartments matched by size/specialty; both receiveMSF+personalHRconsultant feedback atbaseline; onlyintervention gets course.
baseline_and_followup: MSFbaseline andone year after course; course experience ratings postcourse.
attrition_and_missingness: MSF27->20 intervention,15->9control; missing item score replaced with respondent's categorymean; exclusions for noncompletion orleavingCRErole.
blinding_or_independent_rating: Self plus selected head,>=3consultants and>=3trainees; leader selected raters. No blinding documented.
validity_bias_negative_findings: 69-item role-specific measure reportedly validated previously; no fresh psychometric coefficients presented here. Pooling heads/peers/trainees may obscure perspective differences; highbaseline ceiling; feedback itself intervention; convenience selection and differentialattrition. Authors speculate insufficient support/opportunity to enact learning; not measured causal explanations. Null significance does not establish equivalence.

source_passages.excerpt: Although participants reported to have learned from the leadership course no improvement was found.

outcomes.result: Adjusted group comparisonp=.149. Respondentratingintervention5.6->5.6;control5.5->5.7. No demonstrated additionalcourseeffect.

title: A Training Intervention through a 360° Multisource Feedback Model
participants_and_setting: 94 of 127 volunteers from four areas of a Spanish hospital; 13 supervisors and 81 staff.
content_and_delivery: 360 assessment and feedback model during 2016–2018. Supervisors completed one five-hour module; staff completed two three-hour workshops. Meetings followed discrepant feedback.
assignment_and_comparator: Single-group pre/post; noexternal comparator orrandom assignment.
validity_bias_negative_findings: Expert-derived behaviour items; instrument alphas not located. Measurement invariance across raters untested. Ceiling effects persisted despite excluding constant extreme protocols; supervisors generally rated highest. Methods says voluntary 94/127, Discussion says nonvoluntary sample. Complaint correlations do not establish training-caused patient benefit.

source_passages.excerpt: neither the behavioral change in the analyzed competencies
source_passages.note: Opening fragment of sentence reporting no significant supervisor changes.

lead_review_caution: Multiple-source ratings involved feedback/reconciliation meetings; not independent blinded judgments. Staff results-orientation narrative p=.017 conflicts with Table4 double-star footnote p<.01; no corrected p invented.

title: Simulation-Based Team Leadership Training Improves Team Leadership During Actual Trauma Resuscitations: A Randomized Controlled Trial
participants_and_setting: 79 second/third-year emergency medicine and surgery residents randomized; 60 analysed, 30 per arm; 360 actual trauma resuscitations at one US academic level 1 center.
content_and_delivery: Four hours: one-hour didactic, simulations, observation and instructor-led debrief. Targets assuming leadership, interpreting information, prioritizing, assigning roles and seeking input.
validity_bias_negative_findings: Rubric reviewed by ten experts and piloted on five videos; maximum 38, best-effort scoring. Item agreement .9–1.0; care checklist kappa .8 (SD .09). Context-specific measure, not a universal leadership scale. Care measures process adherence, not mortality. Team composition and other members taking leadership not fully controlled; contamination possible. Powered for leadership, not care.

source_passages.excerpt: this study was not powered to detect differences in patient care.

lead_review_caution: Abstract/main-text/table disagreements in effect size and care p value preserved; no preferred number selected.

title: Assessing and measuring leadership identity
discovery_route: S6 -> S7 OA lookup -> institutional PDF
construct: Leader identity: centrality of being a leader in self-concept. Leadership identity: views of leadership, including position-to-process shift and individual, relational, collective aspects.
measure_or_instrument: Discusses LID stage scales, rubrics, Q-sort and reflective methods; proposed three-phase scale still in development.
design: Conceptual/methodological article; no intervention effect or completed validation of proposed scale.
key_evidence: Separates programme evaluation, developmental reflection and research measurement. Recommends explicit goals, multiple waves for developmental research, nonlinear trajectories and contextual qualitative evidence. Prior LID studies are secondary evidence here.
validity_and_limits: Learner talk and behaviour may diverge and multiple stages may appear simultaneously. Do not turn proposed scale into a validated tool. No success cutoff or causal training effect supplied.

source_passages.excerpt: their actual behaviors reﬂect an earlier stage
three or more waves of data

outcomes.rater: Participant reflection; triangulate behaviour where enactment is the goal
outcomes.timing: Repeated waves; recommends at least three for research
outcomes.self_report_or_demonstrated_performance: Identity meaning-making is legitimate; not skill demonstration

lead_inference: Desired identity direction depends on programme purpose; stronger individual leader self-identification is not a universal success criterion.

title: Measuring Leader Identity: Conceptualization and Validation of a Multi-Dimensional Measure
construct: Four leader identity dimensions: strength, integration across life roles, meaning of leadership and inclusiveness/group orientation.
measure_or_instrument: 16-item Leader Identity Measure; four items per dimension; five-point descriptiveness.
design: Three scale studies: 123 undergraduate content classification; 353 higher-level students EFA/CFA and convergence/discrimination; 142 working adults with 84 matched ninety-day follow-ups.
key_evidence: Student alpha .90/.96/.92/.93; split EFA/CFA; four-factor versus one-factor comparison. Ninety-day developmental efficacy associated with strength, integration and inclusiveness; meaning interval includes zero. No training intervention.
validity_and_limits: Three convenience contexts; internal consistency is not workplace competence or training responsiveness. Authors describe good fit, but RMSEA .09 (split sample) and .11 (employees) qualifies claim. Workplace performance and multisource validation left for future. Study3 Table5 labels self-awareness where Methods names self-leadership. No DOI printed; do not invent.

source_passages.excerpt: multi-source reports of important work-place outcomes of leader identity should be examined.

outcomes.validity: Content classification, factors, convergence/discrimination, prospective self-report criterion; no training responsiveness or invariance test located

lead_inference: Psychometric support is distinct from sensitivity to meaningful change, independent workplace prediction and causal training effect.
